name: Damiana extract (Turnera diffusa)
lead: Damiana (Turnera diffusa) is a small, aromatic, woody shrub native to southern Texas, Mexico, Central and South America and the Caribbean. It is traditionally brewed into herbal tea, used in smoking blends and flavored into a Mexican liqueur, and it was an ingredient in several 19th-century patent medicines promoted as an aphrodisiac [1].

In the bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation communities, damiana leaf extract is discussed as a plant-derived aromatase inhibitor. The idea is that blocking aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to estradiol, could lower estrogen-related water retention and soft tissue and leave a leaner, drier, more muscular look. A 2008 laboratory study in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology reported anti-aromatase activity for constituents of the plant, and Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page lists damiana among natural substances reported to act this way [2][3].

Research on damiana is mostly preclinical. Reviews catalogue antioxidant, hepatoprotective, neuroprotective, hypoglycemic and aphrodisiac activities in cell and animal assays and call for clinical trials [10][5]. No human trial of damiana alone on estrogen levels, body composition or appearance has been published.

paras: Damiana is a shrub of the passion-flower family (Passifloraceae) that bears small aromatic flowers in summer, followed by fruit with a fig-like taste. Its leaves have a strong spicy fragrance that is often compared to chamomile [1].

Folklore regards the plant as an aphrodisiac, which is reflected in the old synonym Turnera aphrodisiaca. In the 1800s it appeared in patent medicines such as Pemberton's French Wine Coca, although its leaves were dropped from the non-alcoholic drink that became Coca-Cola. It remains an ingredient of a traditional Mexican liqueur sometimes substituted for triple sec in margaritas, and it is used in herbal teas and smoking blends valued for mild calming effects [1].

A 2014 review of the genus Turnera notes that roughly half a dozen of its 135 accepted species are used in traditional medicine, damiana being the best known. Traditional applications listed include digestive complaints, respiratory problems, pain, diabetes and women's health issues, alongside its aphrodisiac reputation [5].

Damiana shows up in lists of natural aromatase inhibitors and in multi-herb formulations sold for men's vitality. On T Nation, forum members discussed a 2008 study on damiana's anti-aromatase activity in a thread titled for that finding, and users have posted multi-herb 'test boosting' tinctures and multivitamins that include damiana leaf extract [11][12][13]. Members typically describe it as one component of a stack rather than a stand-alone product.

The appearance rationale is indirect: proponents link aromatase inhibition to less estrogen-driven water retention and gynecomastia risk in hormone-focused physique building. Whether oral damiana changes aromatase activity in people has not been measured in published research.

The plant contains flavonoids such as apigenin and acacetin, plus terpenoids, phenolics and cyanogenic glycosides. As of 2006 the constituents responsible for the whole herb's effects had not been identified [1]. The 2014 review counts 22 different flavonoids across the genus Turnera, along with maltol glucoside, seven cyanogenic glycosides, monoterpenoids, sesquiterpenoids, triterpenoids, fatty acids and caffeine [5]. A 2020 review notes that acacetin, a flavone also present in damiana, has been studied for anticancer, anti-inflammatory and other effects in cell and animal models [4]. A 2019 study reported selective inhibition of human monoamine oxidase B by acacetin 7-methyl ether isolated from damiana [14].

A 2008 study from the University of Mississippi tested constituents isolated from damiana in an enzyme assay and reported anti-aromatase activity [2]. The 2014 review lists antiaromatase activity among the bioactivities shown for Turnera species, adding that most of these activities have been examined only in chemical, cell-based or animal assays [5]. Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page notes that damiana extract is reported to suppress aromatase, though it flags the claim as needing better sourcing [3].

A separate 1998 screening of more than 150 herbs measured binding to estrogen and progesterone receptors in human breast cancer cells, a different mechanism from enzyme inhibition [6]. A 2021 review lists Turnera diffusa among plants used traditionally for menopausal symptoms and discussed for estrogenic effects [15].

A 2022 study in skin cells (keratinocytes and fibroblasts) exposed to UVB light reported that damiana leaf extract modulated the AP-1 and Nrf2/ARE pathways, which the authors interpreted as an antiphotoaging effect [16]. A 2025 paper examined damiana in cultured fat cells and muscle cells, reporting reduced adipocyte differentiation and improved glucose uptake in myocytes [17]. These are cell-culture findings. A 2020 review of herbal sexual enhancers includes damiana in its survey of psychiatric and neurological adverse effects reported for such herbs [18].

Damiana is sold as a dietary or herbal supplement. A homeopathic and herbal combination product listing damiana carries label warnings to ask a doctor before use if pregnant or breast-feeding and to stop use if symptoms persist or worsen [7]. The 2020 review of herbal sexual enhancers examined reports of psychiatric and neurological side effects across a group of popular aphrodisiac herbs including damiana [18]. Controlled long-term safety data for damiana extract are limited.

Many plants and seeds sold under the name damiana are actually Turnera ulmifolia, or false damiana, a related species with different chemistry, though Wikipedia says this occurs mostly in horticultural sales [1]. A 2005 survey of herbal supplements marketed on the internet for recreational use examined products of this kind [19].

No studies found on damiana alone for aromatase inhibition, estrogen levels, body composition or appearance. Related human research tested multi-ingredient products: a 2001 double-blind trial of the ArginMax supplement (which contains damiana among other ingredients) in female sexual function [8], and a 2001 randomized trial of a South American herbal preparation in overweight patients, which reported weight loss and delayed gastric emptying [9]. A registered 2008 study (n=19) compared an herbal combination containing yerba mate, guarana and damiana with other components for appetite suppression [20]. These products cannot isolate damiana's contribution.

lore.intro: Damiana is discussed on T Nation and similar forums mainly as a possible natural aromatase inhibitor and as an ingredient in herbal testosterone-support blends [11][12][13].

claims.claim: Damiana is a natural aromatase inhibitor
claims.believers: Forum members point to the 2008 Journal of Ethnopharmacology paper and to acacetin's reported moderate aromatase inhibition as the basis for using damiana to limit estrogen conversion [11][12].
claims.experts: The 2008 study and a 2014 review describe anti-aromatase activity in laboratory assays; no human trial has measured aromatase or estradiol after damiana use [2][5].

claims.claim: Damiana raises libido and supports testosterone-oriented stacks
claims.believers: Users include damiana in multi-herb tinctures and multivitamins alongside ginseng, eleuthero and cordyceps, citing its aphrodisiac tradition [13].
claims.experts: A 2023 review rates aphrodisiac activity among the more promising reported effects but notes that clinical trials are needed; the one human trial found used a multi-ingredient product [10][8].

card.summary: A traditional aphrodisiac herb with a lab report of anti-aromatase constituents and no human trials of the extract on its own.
card.note: Products may be mislabelled with a related species.

quick.overview:
Damiana is a shrub used in teas and liqueurs and sold as an herbal supplement. It is mentioned online as a natural aromatase inhibitor.
The basis is a 2008 laboratory study of its constituents; no human trial of damiana alone on estrogen or appearance was found.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids such as pinocembrin and acacetin are reported to inhibit aromatase in lab assays.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited. Products may contain false damiana (Turnera ulmifolia), and combination products make effects hard to attribute.

chain: Leaf extract contains flavonoids such as acacetin and pinocembrin
Lab assays show these compounds inhibiting the aromatase enzyme
Less testosterone-to-estradiol conversion is the hoped-for result
Lower estrogen-related softness and water retention
angle.text: Users take damiana extract hoping its flavonoids will modestly slow aromatase, so that more testosterone stays as testosterone and estrogen-related water retention and fat gain are reduced. This chain rests on laboratory findings; human outcomes have not been measured.
